extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students in algebraic topology; researchers needing reference on Poincaré duality, Alexander duality, and universal coefficient/homology algebra
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook section on Poincaré duality and related dualities (Lefschetz, Alexander), cup-product structures (lens spaces, middle-dimensional pairings), collars and manifolds with boundary, and the universal coefficient theorem for homology including Tor. Contains statements, proofs, examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology generators of lens spaces (finite coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: H_j(L^{2n+1}; Z_m) is generated by β^i for j = 2i and by αβ^i for j = 2i+1, where α ∈ H^1(L^{2n+1}; Z_m) and β ∈ H^2(L^{2n+1}; Z_m) are generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction using inclusion L^{2n-1} ⊂ L^{2n+1} and behavior of maps h : H^i(–; Z_m) → Hom(H_i(–; Z_m), Z_m). If an integer k appears in expressing a top generator it must be relatively prime to m, so αβ^n and β^n generate the top groups accordingly. The infinite-dimensional lens space ring and passage from Z_m to Z coefficients are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cup product structure in lens spaces (α^2 behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rest of the cup product structure on H^*(L^{2n+1}; Z_m) is determined once α^2 is expressed as a multiple of β. When m is odd, commutativity implies α^2 = 0. When m is even, α^2 is either 0 or the unique element of H^2(L^{2n+1}; Z_m) ≈ Z_m of order two; in fact for the 2-skeleton the nontrivial option holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses the 2-skeleton L^2 (circle with a 2-cell attached by degree m) and the cup product computation in that 2-complex (Example 3.9). Note one cannot deduce nontriviality of α^2 from Poincaré duality alone except when m = 2. The infinite lens space ring H^*(L^∞; Z) ≈ Z[α]/(mα) with |α| = 2 is described and finite case obtained by setting α^{n+1}=0 and adjoining extra Z in top dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle-dimensional cup product pairing for closed orientable 2n-manifolds
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed orientable manifold M of dimension 2n, the middle-dimensional cup product pairing H^n_free(M) × H^n_free(M) → Z is a nonsingular bilinear form on the torsionfree part H^n_free(M). This form is symmetric when n is even and skew-symmetric when n is odd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the skew-symmetric case the form can be put in standard 2×2 block form with blocks [[0,1],[-1,0]] so the rank of H^n(M^{2n}) must be even when n is odd. The symmetric case is more intricate: up to isomorphism there are finitely many symmetric nonsingular bilinear forms over Z of a fixed rank; realizability results in certain dimensions (4, 8, 16) and relations to manifold classification (e.g., simply-connected closed 4-manifolds) are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of collars for compact manifolds with boundary (Proposition 3.42)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a compact manifold with boundary, then ∂M has a collar neighborhood: an open neighborhood homeomorphic to ∂M × [0,1) taking ∂M to ∂M × {0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs an external collar and a homeomorphism M → M' by finite partition of unity on ∂M, local half-space charts, and piecewise stretching homeomorphisms whose composition produces the required collar. More generally collars can be constructed for boundaries of paracompact manifolds similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: boundary of an n-manifold and points characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: An n-manifold with boundary is a Hausdorff space where each point has a neighborhood homeomorphic either to R^n or to the half-space R^n_+ = {(x1,…,xn) | xn ≥ 0}. Points x with H_n(M, M − {x}; Z) = 0 form the boundary ∂M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ∂R^n_+ = R^{n-1}, ∂D^n = S^{n-1}. This characterization via local homology is used to define collars and relative fundamental classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: R-orientability and relative fundamental class for manifolds with boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: A compact manifold M with boundary is R-orientable if M − ∂M is R-orientable as a manifold without boundary. When ∂M × [0,1) is a collar neighborhood, Hi(M, ∂M; R) ≈ Hi(M − ∂M, ∂M × (0,ε); R) and Lemma 3.27 gives a relative fundamental class [M] ∈ H_n(M, ∂M; R) restricting to a chosen orientation on M − ∂M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relative fundamental class is the input for duality isomorphisms (Lefschetz duality / Theorem 3.43).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lefschetz duality generalization for manifolds with boundary (Theorem 3.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose M is a compact R-orientable n-manifold whose boundary ∂M is decomposed as the union of two compact (n−1)-manifolds A and B with common boundary ∂A = ∂B = A ∩ B. Then cap product with a fundamental class [M] ∈ H_n(M, ∂M; R) gives isomorphisms D_M: H^k(M, A; R) → H_{n−k}(M, B; R) for all k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence of collar neighborhoods implies A and B deformation-retract onto neighborhoods, reducing to earlier Poincaré duality results; proof uses five-lemma on the relevant diagram and checks compatibility of boundary maps sending fundamental classes to fundamental classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duality for compact locally contractible subspaces (Theorem 3.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is a compact, locally contractible subspace of a closed orientable n-manifold M, then H_i(M, M − K; Z) ≈ H^{n−i}(K; Z) for all i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses neighborhoods U of K, long exact sequences of pairs, Poincaré duality on complements, passage to direct limits over neighborhoods, and retracting neighborhoods to K using embedding/retraction results (Appendix theorems). This leads to Alexander duality as an immediate corollary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alexander duality (Corollary 3.45)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is a compact, locally contractible, nonempty, proper subspace of S^n, then H_i(S^n − K; Z) ≈ H^{n−i−1}(K; Z) for all i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Theorem 3.44 and the long exact sequence of the pair (S^n, S^n − K). The short exact sequence exception for i = n−1 is explained and shown to split by comparison with the case K a point. Remarks highlight that homology of the complement depends only on K, not on embedding pathologies, provided K is locally contractible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary on cohomology of compact locally contractible subsets of R^n (Corollary 3.46)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ R^n is compact and locally contractible then H^i(X; Z) = 0 for i ≥ n and is torsionfree for i = n−1 and n−2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Alexander duality to relate H^i(X) to homology of complements and the universal coefficient theorem; examples show embedding obstructions (e.g., nonorientable n-manifold cannot embed in R^{n+1}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Čech cohomology via nerves of covers (definition and comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Čech cohomology ˇH^i(X; G) is defined as the direct limit lim_{→} H^i(N(U); G) over nerves N(U) of open covers U of X, where N(U) is the simplicial nerve of the cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For spaces homotopy equivalent to CW complexes, Čech cohomology coincides with singular cohomology. For spaces with local complexities it behaves better (example: shrinking wedge of spheres: singular H^3(X; Z) nonzero but ˇH^3(X; Z) = 0 and ˇH^2(X; Z) = ⊕_{countable} Z). Čech homology (inverse limits) is less well-behaved due to failure of exactness; Steenrod homology is a remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain complexes with coefficients and tensor product description
rubrics_metrics.description: For a space X and abelian group G, the chain group C_n(X; G) is naturally isomorphic to C_n(X) ⊗ G, and similarly for relative chains C_n(X, A; G) ≈ C_n(X, A) ⊗ G, with boundary map ∂ ⊗ 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic identification reduces computation of homology with arbitrary coefficients to algebraic questions about tensoring chain complexes of free abelian groups with G, motivating the universal coefficient theorem for homology and the Tor functor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal coefficient theorem for homology (Theorem 3A.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is a chain complex of free abelian groups, then for all n and all G there are natural split short exact sequences 0 → H_n(C) ⊗ G → H_n(C; G) → Tor(H_{n−1}(C), G) → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequences are natural with respect to chain maps and split (but not naturally). The splitting is obtained by choosing projections C_n → Z_n and producing a chain map C → H(C) (regarded with trivial differentials) and tensoring. Corollary 3A.4 gives the analogous sequence for singular homology of pairs (X,A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic properties of Tor (Tor_n(H,G))
rubrics_metrics.description: Tor_n(H,G) is defined as H_n(F ⊗ G) for any free resolution F → H → 0; Tor_n(H,G) is independent of the chosen free resolution. For abelian groups Tor_n(H,G) = 0 for n > 1; Tor_1(H,G) is typically denoted Tor(H,G), and Tor_0(H,G) ≈ H ⊗ G under an augmented convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tor measures common torsion of H and G. Construction and functoriality (in both arguments) are discussed. Explicit calculations and properties follow in Proposition 3A.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of Tor (Proposition 3A.5 parts (1)-(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Key properties: (1) Tor(A,B) ≈ Tor(B,A). (2) Tor(⊕_i A_i, B) ≈ ⊕_i Tor(A_i,B). (3) Tor(A,B)=0 if A or B is free, or more generally torsionfree. (4) Tor(A,B) ≈ Tor(T(A),B) where T(A) is the torsion subgroup of A. (5) Tor(Z_n, A) ≈ Ker(A -n→ A) (kernel of multiplication by n on A). (6) For each short exact sequence 0→B→C→D→0 there is an associated six-term exact sequence 0→Tor(A,B)→Tor(A,C)→Tor(A,D)→A⊗B→A⊗C→A⊗D→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use free resolutions, tensor product exactness properties, and reduction to finitely generated/torsion cases. Example: Tor(Z_m, Z_n) ≈ Z_{gcd(m,n)}; for finitely generated groups Tor(A,B) is (roughly) the tensor product of torsion subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for homology with field coefficients (Corollary 3A.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) H_n(X; Q) ≈ H_n(X; Z) ⊗ Q, so when H_n(X; Z) is finitely generated, dim_Q H_n(X; Q) equals rank of H_n(X; Z). (b) If H_n(X; Z) and H_{n−1}(X; Z) are finitely generated, then for p prime, H_n(X; Z_p) consists of ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begins analysis of homology with field coefficients using the universal coefficient theorem; part (b) continues beyond the chunk given. The corollary shows taking Q-coefficients retains rank information but loses torsion.
